He too was thrown out by a Constitutional Court ruling. A career politician, Abhisit was born in Newcastle in the north east of England to wealthy Thai-Chinese parents and attended Eton, one of the UK's top private schools before studying politics, philosophy and economics at Oxford University. While highly critical of the corruption and cronyism in Thai politics, Abhisit's own route to power has not been as he may have wanted it. As leader of the Democrat Party since 2005, he failed to win either of the elections he contended. He was chosen by the Thai parliament to be Prime Minister during a special session. His selection was contingent on support of factions from the now banned PPP who changed allegiance, many of whom he had previously criticized. Abhisit now leads a coalition government with a small majority consisting of a number of parties and interests, leading political commentators to speculate about the length of his tenure in office, many suggesting more than a year in power would be a success. Countering accusations of inexperience, Abhisit can still boast 17 years of political practice, having become a parliamentarian at the age of 27. As well as being young and cosmopolitan, he has gained a reputation as being above the sleaze and corruption that has dogged many other Thai politicians, while he publicly opposed the bloodless military coup that removed Thaksin from office 2006. However critics have said that his policies are borrowed heavily from Thaksin and that his party's decision to boycott the snap election in 2006 led to the constitutional crisis and coup against Thaksin. Most of Abhisit's support comes from the educated middle classes and gaining support, or at least lessening the divisions between sections of Thai society is something he has been immediately faced with. "He needs to send a clear signal of change that he is a leader who will reach out to all," said Bunranaj Smutharak, a spokesman for Abhisit's Democrat Party. "We are confident the long turmoil over the past two years will be brought to an end by this change in government," he said. "What we set out to do is reunite the country."

# Abhisit Vejjajiva: Thailand's Youngest Prime Minister in Six Decades

At just 44 years old, Abhisit Vejjajiva assumed the role of Thailand's prime minister, becoming the youngest person to hold the office in more than 60 years. His ascension was equally remarkable for its timing, as he became the country's third prime minister in a span of just four months—a testament to the extraordinary political instability gripping the nation.

## A Nation in Turmoil

Thailand's political upheaval, marked by widespread national demonstrations and the dramatic closure of the country's airports, can be traced back to the 2006 military coup that overthrew former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra. The fallout from that event continued to reverberate through Thai politics for years, destabilizing successive governments and deepening divisions within the country.

The rapid turnover in leadership underscored the depth of this crisis. Two of Abhisit's immediate predecessors, Samak Sundaravej and Somchai Wongsawat, were both forced from office by rulings handed down by the Constitutional Court, further illustrating the fragile state of Thai governance during this turbulent period.

## An Unconventional Background

Abhisit's personal history sets him apart from many of his political contemporaries. Born in England and educated at some of Britain's most prestigious institutions—Eton College and the University of Oxford—he brought a distinctly international background to Thai politics. As a career politician, he rose to lead the Democrat Party, though notably he had lost both of the elections he had previously contested.

## Rise to Power

Despite his electoral setbacks, Abhisit was ultimately selected as prime minister by parliament. His appointment was secured with crucial support from factions of the banned People's Power Party (PPP), enabling him to form a coalition government. However, his administration was built on a narrow foundation, commanding only a small majority—a reflection of the precarious political landscape he inherited and the challenges that lay ahead.

# Political Turmoil and Transition in Thailand

Thailand, long regarded as one of Southeast Asia's more stable democracies, descended into a prolonged period of political instability in the years following the September 2006 military coup that removed Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra from power. Thaksin, a billionaire businessman turned populist leader, had commanded strong support among the rural poor, but his tenure was marked by mounting accusations of corruption, abuse of power, and authoritarian tendencies. His ouster, rather than resolving the nation's deep divisions, exposed and deepened them, setting the stage for years of confrontation between his supporters and opponents.

## A Revolving Door of Leadership

The instability that followed was striking in its intensity. Over the course of just four months, Thailand cycled through three prime ministers, each forced from office amid a combination of mass street demonstrations and adverse rulings from the Constitutional Court. Successive governments aligned with Thaksin's political movement found themselves unable to hold power, as the judiciary and organized protest movements repeatedly intervened to bring down sitting leaders. This turbulence paralyzed governance, unsettled the economy, and eroded confidence in the country's democratic institutions, leaving Thailand in a state of persistent uncertainty.

## The Rise of Abhisit Vejjajiva

The turmoil culminated on December 15, when Abhisit Vejjajiva, leader of the Democrat Party, was named prime minister. Oxford-educated and articulate, Abhisit represented a marked contrast to the populist style that had dominated Thai politics in the preceding years. At just 44 years old, he became the youngest person to hold the office in more than six decades, a milestone that underscored both the generational shift he embodied and the extraordinary circumstances that brought him to power.

## Challenges Ahead

Yet Abhisit's ascension came burdened with formidable challenges. His most pressing task was to restore stability to a nation that had once been a model of relative political continuity but was now fractured by years of conflict. Complicating this mission was the fragile nature of his own position. His government rested on a coalition held together by shifting political allegiances and pragmatic alliances—precisely the kind of opportunistic maneuvering he had criticized when it served his opponents. This contradiction placed Abhisit in a precarious position, tasked with unifying a divided country while depending on the very political arrangements whose legitimacy he had previously questioned. Whether he could translate his credentials and ambitions into lasting stability remained an open and pressing question.

**BANGKOK, Thailand** — Thailand's Parliament has elected Abhisit Vejjajiva as the nation's new prime minister, elevating the youthful, British-educated opposition leader to the top office amid one of the most turbulent periods in the country's recent political history.

At 44, Abhisit becomes one of Thailand's youngest prime ministers, inheriting a nation deeply polarized by years of political conflict, mass street protests, and economic uncertainty.

## A Privileged and International Background

Born in Newcastle, England, in 1964 to a family of Thai physicians of Chinese-Vietnamese descent, Abhisit's biography stands in sharp contrast to many of his predecessors. He was educated at Eton College, one of Britain's most prestigious schools, before earning degrees in philosophy, politics, and economics at Oxford University.

His polished, articulate demeanor and fluent English have made him a favorite among Thailand's urban middle class and business elite. Before entering politics, he briefly taught at a Thai military academy and lectured in economics.

Abhisit rose through the ranks of the Democrat Party, Thailand's oldest political party, eventually becoming its leader. He has cultivated an image as a clean, reform-minded politician untainted by the corruption allegations that have dogged many Thai political figures.

## The Road to Power

Abhisit's ascension follows years of chaos that toppled governments aligned with former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, the telecommunications billionaire ousted in a 2006 military coup.

Thaksin, who remains a deeply divisive figure, drew fierce loyalty from rural and working-class voters in Thailand's north and northeast, who benefited from his populist policies. But he alienated the Bangkok establishment, the military, and urban elites who accused him of corruption and authoritarianism.

The most recent crisis unfolded when the anti-Thaksin "yellow shirt" movement — the People's Alliance for Democracy — staged prolonged protests, culminating in the seizure of Bangkok's two airports. The blockade stranded thousands of travelers and dealt a severe blow to Thailand's vital tourism industry.

The turmoil reached a turning point when a court dissolved the ruling pro-Thaksin People Power Party over electoral fraud, banning its leaders from politics. This ruling created the opening that allowed Abhisit's Democrat Party to assemble a governing coalition, partly by winning over factions that had previously supported the government.

## Challenges Ahead

Abhisit takes office facing formidable obstacles. Critics — particularly the "red shirt" supporters of Thaksin — argue that his government lacks legitimacy, having come to power through parliamentary maneuvering and court decisions rather than a direct electoral mandate.

The new prime minister must also confront a slowing economy battered by both the global financial crisis and the domestic political instability, along with a long-running insurgency in Thailand's Muslim-majority southern provinces.

Perhaps his greatest challenge will be healing the deep divisions between Thailand's urban and rural populations that have fueled years of unrest.

"The country has been through a very difficult time," Abhisit said following his election. He pledged to restore stability and address the economic hardships facing ordinary Thais.

Whether the young leader can bridge Thailand's political fault lines — or whether he will become the latest casualty of the nation's cyclical unrest — remains to be seen.

---

# Thailand's Descent into Political Turmoil: 2006-2008

## A Nation Divided

Between 2006 and 2008, Thailand experienced one of the most turbulent periods in its modern political history—a crisis marked by a military coup, mass street protests, judicial interventions, and the collapse of multiple governments. At its heart lay a deep societal fracture between competing visions of Thai democracy and power.

## The 2006 Coup

The crisis crystallized on September 19, 2006, when the Royal Thai Army, led by General Sonthi Boonyaratglin, seized power in a bloodless coup while Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra was in New York attending a UN General Assembly meeting.

Thaksin, a telecommunications billionaire, had won landslide electoral victories in 2001 and 2005, building unprecedented popularity among rural and working-class Thais through populist policies including affordable healthcare and village development funds. However, his tenure was dogged by allegations of corruption, abuse of power, conflicts of interest, and authoritarian tendencies—particularly a controversial "war on drugs" that resulted in thousands of extrajudicial killings.

The coup enjoyed support from Bangkok's urban middle class, royalist establishment, and elements aligned with the monarchy and traditional bureaucracy. The military junta, styling itself the Council for National Security, abrogated the 2007 constitution and installed an interim government.

## A New Constitution and Return to Elections

The junta oversaw the drafting of a new constitution, approved by referendum in 2007, which contained provisions widely seen as designed to weaken large political parties like Thaksin's. Meanwhile, Thaksin's Thai Rak Thai party was dissolved by a court ruling, and its executives banned from politics for five years.

Despite these measures, when elections were held in December 2007, the pro-Thaksin People's Power Party (PPP)—effectively a reincarnation of Thai Rak Thai—won a decisive victory. Samak Sundaravej became prime minister, demonstrating the enduring loyalty of Thaksin's electoral base.

## The Yellow Shirts and Street Politics

The PPP's return to power reignited opposition from the People's Alliance for Democracy (PAD), whose supporters became known as the "Yellow Shirts" for the color symbolizing loyalty to the monarchy. The PAD accused the government of being a proxy for the exiled Thaksin and staged prolonged protests throughout 2008.

The Yellow Shirts controversially advocated for a "New Politics" that would reduce the influence of elected representatives—reflecting elite anxieties about the political power of the rural majority.

## Judicial Interventions and Government Instability

The judiciary emerged as a decisive force in what critics termed a "judicial coup." In September 2008, the Constitutional Court removed Prime Minister Samak from office over a technicality—his paid appearances on a television cooking show, ruled a conflict of interest.

Samak was succeeded by Somchai Wongsawat, Thaksin's brother-in-law, further inflaming opposition. The political temperature rose dangerously as clashes between protesters and authorities turned violent.

## Airport Occupation and Government Collapse

The crisis reached a dramatic climax in late November 2008 when Yellow Shirt protesters seized Bangkok's two airports—Suvarnabhumi and Don Mueang—stranding hundreds of thousands of travelers and inflicting severe damage on Thailand's tourism-dependent economy and international reputation.

The standoff ended on December 2, 2008, when the Constitutional Court dissolved the People's Power Party and two coalition partners for electoral fraud, disqualifying Somchai and banning party executives from politics. The Yellow Shirts declared victory and ended their airport occupation.

## Abhisit Takes Power

With the pro-Thaksin coalition fractured, political maneuvering—reportedly with military encouragement—led a faction to defect and join the opposition Democrat Party. On December 15, 2008, parliament voted Abhisit Vejjajiva, the Oxford-educated Democrat leader, as prime minister.

For opponents, Abhisit's ascension represented a restoration of stability. But for Thaksin's supporters, it symbolized how their electoral victories could be repeatedly overturned through extra-parliamentary means—a grievance that would fuel the "Red Shirt" movement and continue Thailand's political struggles for years to come.

## An Unresolved Divide

The 2006-2008 period exposed a fundamental tension in Thai society: between the electoral power of the rural and working-class majority and the entrenched influence of Bangkok's traditional elites, military, and royalist establishment. Far from resolving this conflict, Abhisit's appointment merely set the stage for further confrontations, underscoring that Thailand's political crisis was rooted in deep structural divisions no single government could easily bridge.

His polished English and cosmopolitan background earned him the nickname "Mark," a moniker that has followed him throughout his political career.

Abhisit entered Thai politics through the Democrat Party, the country's oldest political party, and quickly distinguished himself as a rising star. He became one of the youngest members of parliament and eventually ascended to lead the party.

His path to the premiership, however, was anything but conventional. **The 2010 crackdown:** Perhaps the most serious criticism stems from the government's handling of the massive "Red Shirt" protests in 2010, when anti-government demonstrators occupied central Bangkok for weeks. The military crackdown that ended the protests resulted in numerous deaths and injuries, leaving a deep scar on the national psyche and raising difficult questions about the use of force against civilians.

**The elite disconnect:** Critics have characterized Abhisit as representing Thailand's traditional Bangkok-based establishment—the urban elite, military, and royalist factions—while remaining disconnected from the rural poor who formed the backbone of Thaksin's support base. His privileged upbringing and foreign education, while impressive, have at times been used to paint him as out of touch with ordinary Thais.

**Perceived military dependence:** Some observers have questioned the extent to which his government relied upon and was beholden to military backing.

## A Nation Divided

Abhisit governs a country split along stark lines—between the Red Shirts loyal to Thaksin and the Yellow Shirts of the establishment, between urban and rural, between competing visions of Thailand's democratic future. His interview with Dan Rivers offers an opportunity to address these divisions and defend his record before an international audience.

As he faces CNN's questions, the central tension of his premiership remains: Can an Oxford-educated technocrat with establishment ties bridge the profound divides tearing at Thailand's social fabric?

---

# Abhisit Vejjajiva's Ascension: Thailand's Political Turbulence of 2008

## Executive Summary

In December 2008, Abhisit Vejjajiva of the Democrat Party became Thailand's Prime Minister, marking the third change in the nation's leadership within a single year. His rise to power occurred against a backdrop of extraordinary political instability, mass street protests, judicial interventions, and the lingering influence of exiled former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra. This report examines the sequence of events that led to Abhisit's appointment and the broader political dynamics that shaped this turbulent period.

## Background: The Thaksin Legacy

To understand the events of 2008, one must first recognize the polarizing figure of **Thaksin Shinawatra**. A telecommunications billionaire, Thaksin served as Prime Minister from 2001 to 2006, building a formidable political base through populist policies that appealed particularly to rural voters in Thailand's north and northeast. His government provided affordable healthcare, agricultural subsidies, and village development funds.

However, Thaksin's tenure was marred by allegations of corruption, cronyism, and authoritarian tendencies. He faced fierce opposition from Bangkok's urban middle class, royalist establishment, and the military. In September 2006, while Thaksin was abroad, the military staged a coup that removed him from power. He subsequently went into self-imposed exile to avoid corruption charges.

Despite his physical absence, Thaksin's political influence remained potent, embodied by successor parties and loyal proxies who continued to command significant electoral support.

## The First Successor: Samak Sundaravej

Following the 2007 elections, the **People's Power Party (PPP)**—widely viewed as a reincarnation of Thaksin's disbanded Thai Rak Thai party—emerged victorious. **Samak Sundaravej**, a veteran right-wing politician, became Prime Minister in early 2008.

Samak openly acknowledged himself as a proxy for Thaksin, which galvanized opposition from the **People's Alliance for Democracy (PAD)**, also known as the "Yellow Shirts." The PAD, backed by royalist and nationalist elements, launched sustained protests, occupying government buildings and demanding Samak's resignation.

Samak's downfall came from an unexpected quarter. In September 2008, Thailand's Constitutional Court ruled that he had violated the constitution by hosting a paid cooking television program while serving as Prime Minister. This technical violation of conflict-of-interest rules forced him from office, demonstrating the increasingly prominent role of judicial intervention in Thai politics—a phenomenon sometimes termed "judicial coups."

## The Second Successor: Somchai Wongsawat

The PPP quickly nominated **Somchai Wongsawat** as Samak's replacement. Notably, Somchai was Thaksin's brother-in-law, further cementing perceptions that Thaksin continued to control the government from abroad.

Somchai's brief tenure was defined by escalating crisis:

- The PAD intensified its protests, culminating in the dramatic **occupation of Bangkok's Suvarnabhumi and Don Mueang airports** in late November 2008. This blockade stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers and severely damaged Thailand's economy and international reputation.

- Political violence increased, with clashes between protesters and security forces.

- The government appeared paralyzed, unable to resolve the standoff.

Somchai's government met its end through another judicial ruling. On **December 2, 2008**, the Constitutional Court dissolved the People's Power Party, along with two coalition partners, on grounds of electoral fraud committed during the 2007 elections. The ruling banned Somchai and other party executives from politics for five years, effectively removing him from the premiership.

## Abhisit's Path to Power

With the PPP dissolved, the political landscape shifted dramatically. The dissolution created an opening that the opposition **Democrat Party**, Thailand's oldest political party, moved swiftly to exploit.

**Abhisit Vejjajiva**, the Oxford-educated leader of the Democrat Party, emerged as the alternative candidate. Several factors enabled his ascension:

1. **Coalition Realignment**: Crucially, a faction of former PPP members led by Newin Chidchob—previously a Thaksin ally—defected and threw their support behind the Democrats. This defection provided the parliamentary numbers necessary to form a new government.

2. **Parliamentary Vote**: On **December 15, 2008**, the Thai Parliament voted to elect Abhisit as Prime Minister, defeating the candidate put forward by the remnants of the pro-Thaksin bloc.

3. **Establishment Support**: Abhisit enjoyed backing from the military, bureaucratic, and royalist establishment, who viewed him as a stabilizing figure and counterweight to Thaksin's influence.

Abhisit thus became Thailand's youngest Prime Minister in decades, and the third person to hold the office within a single tumultuous year.

## Analysis and Implications

Abhisit's rise revealed several enduring features of Thai politics:

- **The Thaksin Divide**: The events underscored the deep polarization between pro-Thaksin forces (the "Red Shirts") and the anti-Thaksin establishment (the "Yellow Shirts").

- **Judicial Activism**: The successive removals of Samak and Somchai through court rulings highlighted the judiciary's decisive—and controversial—role in shaping political outcomes.

- **Questions of Legitimacy**: Because Abhisit came to power through parliamentary maneuvering rather than a general election victory, his opponents challenged his democratic legitimacy. Pro-Thaksin forces argued that the courts and military had effectively engineered his rise, circumventing the electoral will.

## Aftermath

Abhisit's premiership, which lasted until 2011, was itself beset by instability. In 2010, massive Red Shirt protests in Bangkok led to violent confrontations with the military, resulting in significant casualties. The underlying divisions that brought him to power remained unresolved, foreshadowing continued political turmoil in the years that followed.

## Conclusion

Abhisit Vejjajiva's ascension to the premiership in December 2008 was the product of an extraordinary confluence of judicial interventions, mass protests, and shifting political alliances. The rapid succession from Samak Sundaravej to Somchai Wongsawat to Abhisit within four months illustrated the profound instability generated by the ongoing struggle over Thaksin Shinawatra's legacy—a struggle that would continue to define Thai politics for years to come.
